Entries.Text: Select a behavior file (Behavior category) to browse it here.
Select a behavior file (Behavior category) to see its state machines here.
The behavior as a tree of its state machines, states and generators. Right-click a node for Add Animation, Clone State and Add Transition.
One row per animation selector (CMSG), with its animation ID, state, clips, and what the character has for it.
Every state machine in the file.
Every animation selector (CMSG) in the file.
Every animation clip in the file.
The behavior's variables, with the bindings that use each one. Add Variable is here.
Mistakes that make the game crash or silently do nothing: missing indices, mismatched lists, duplicate state IDs, broken bindings.
Back to the state machine this one was opened from.
Select something in a state machine to show it.

Show the state machine of whatever is selected in the Outline.

In the graph: links are transitions from one state to another (hover for their events). Wildcard transitions, which can be taken from any state, are listed on the state they lead to (* events). Double-click a state whose generator is a state machine to open it. Drag from a state's Out to another state to add a transition.
Reached from any state on {0} events:

Add a clip to this selector for another animation category (aCCC_ plus the selector's animation ID). The clip copies one of the selector's clips, and is given an animation name entry if the animation is new to the file.
Copy this state into the same state machine, with a new name and state ID. Its transitions out are copied; transitions into it aren't.
Add a transition to a state on an event, from one state or from any state (a wildcard transition). The event can be a new one.
Add a variable, with its info, bounds and initial value kept in step.
The animation category: the aCCC in aCCC_YYYYYY. For the player, each category has its own time act (a000, a020 ...).

Off: generators also used outside this state stay shared, so the copy refers to the same ones (an edit to them changes both).
On: everything below the state is copied.

Transition effects always stay shared.
A wildcard transition can be taken from any state of the machine, and is how most of the game's transitions are made.
The variable's value when the behavior starts.
Starts at zero (vector, quaternion as identity) or null (pointer). Edit it afterwards in the Variables tab.

{0} isn't used by any clip in this behavior yet. In this game the behbnd's character file (Characters/cXXXX.hkx, m_animationBundleNameData) lists every animation the behavior uses, so add {0} there first. Adding a clip for an animation the behavior already uses works here.

Remove this reference to the selected object. It's still used in {0} other places. Can be undone.

Remove this reference to the selected object. It's the only one, so the object leaves the file. Can be undone.

Removing a state leaves any transitions to it pointing at a missing state; the Problems tab lists those.

What {0} has for {1}: a time act entry (its events), and an animation file in its anibnds.

A missing one isn't always a mistake. Shared graphs like c9997 name animations most characters don't have, and the game skips those.
Show {0} in the Time Act Editor.

The animations of {0} with a time act entry for this ID. With an offset type other than None, the game picks the category at runtime (from the weapon, stance or magic), so any of these can play.
Only show selectors with a clip whose animation file this character doesn't have.

Click to edit this selector. Double-click to show it in the Outline.

Time Acts: the categories with a time act entry for the animation ID.
Files: the clips whose animation file this character has.

Check the file again.

Checked: event, variable, character property and state indices; the lengths of the lists kept alongside the name lists; duplicate state IDs; clip internal IDs against their animation names; binding member paths.

The game's own files pass every check, so anything listed comes from an edit.

The variable's name, at index {0} in the behavior graph's variable names.
The variable's initial word value. For vector and pointer variables, this is the index of its value in the quad or variant value list.
The objects whose fields are set from this variable.
Copy this and what's below it. A copy held by a state goes into a new state of the same state machine; a copy held by a selector's list goes at the end of that list.
Remove this from every place that holds it. If a state holds it, the state is deleted too, with the transitions into that state.
Drive one of this object's fields from a behavior variable.
Stop a field of this object being driven by a variable or character property.
Add a copy of the selected variable (type, bounds and initial value) at the end of the list. Its bindings aren't copied.
Remove the selected variable and the bindings to it. The variables after it move down one, and every index to them follows.
This object has no fields a variable can drive.
The field the variable sets. Fields that are already bound show their binding. Fields inside sub-objects (such as hands:0/controlData) can be bound in the property grid.
A {0} variable may not suit a {1} field.
This field is already bound: its binding will be changed to this variable.
The copy's m_animId. If it changes, the selector's clips are copied and pointed at the new animation (same categories).

Copy for Paste. Clips, selectors and state machines can only be pasted into the file they were copied from.
Copy this variable for Paste. It can be pasted into any behavior file.

Clips go into the selected selector (or the selected clip's selector) for their category, or the next free one. Selectors and state machines go where the selected selector or state machine is held, as Duplicate would place them. Variables go at the end of the variable list.
Clips, selectors and state machines can only be pasted into the file they were copied from.
